summary: This informational document analyzes the security of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) according to the guidelines in Section 4.2 of RFC 6518, the Keying and Authentication for Routing Protocols (KARP) design guidelines.

eli5.summary: This checks how well the link health check protocol protects itself and what is missing, using a checklist for routing protocol security.

questions: what is a bfd replay attack
subtitle: A gap analysis of BFD's authentication: replay holes, aging algorithms and CPU costs, measured against the KARP guidelines.

tldr.problem: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) is used by routing protocols for liveness checks, but its authentication has weak algorithms, incomplete replay protection and a high cost at millisecond rates.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC checks BFD against the requirements in the KARP guidelines (RFC 6518), explains where replay attacks get through, and suggests improvements such as GMAC and authenticating only state-changing packets.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem analysis, not a protocol change. The ideas are suggestions, and the GMAC and selective-authentication ideas are described as needing more discussion or being a candidate.

facts.label: Rollover example
facts.value: under 24 weeks at one increment per 3.3 ms

today: RFC 7492 is an Informational analysis and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the RFC metadata. It documents gaps in BFD authentication as of 2015 and does not itself change the protocol.

sections.title: Why Analyse BFD Security
sections.content:
This document is a gap analysis of Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (RFC 5880) against the KARP design guidelines (RFC 6518). An earlier analysis of cryptographic issues for routing protocols appeared in RFC 6039.

BFD offers a basic solution: a Key ID lets the key change on demand, and two algorithms, MD5 and SHA-1, protect control packets. Both are shown to be subject to collision attacks. This matters because routing protocols such as RIPv2, IS-IS and OSPFv2 use BFD for liveness checks. If they move to a stronger algorithm while BFD stays weak, an attacker could bring down BFD to bring down the routing protocol.
sections.eli5: If the guard at the gate has a flimsy lock while the vault has a strong one, a thief just picks the gate lock. BFD must be as strong as the things that rely on it.

sections.title: Requirements BFD Does Not Meet
sections.content:
Three requirements from RFC 6862 are not met by BFD. Replay protection: BFD gives incomplete protection within a session and none between sessions, which opens denial-of-service opportunities. Strong algorithms: MD5 and SHA-1 are both vulnerable to collision attacks, and two drafts proposed HMAC with the SHA-2 family.

Preventing DoS attacks: BFD packets can be sent at millisecond intervals, and malicious packets with the authentication bit set can cause a DoS attack. There is no lightweight mechanism in BFD to handle this, which the RFC gives as one reason authentication is still not widely deployed in the field.
sections.eli5: The checklist says BFD should catch replayed messages, use strong locks, and not be easy to overload. It currently misses all three.

sections.title: How BFD Authentication Works Today
sections.content:
BFD defines five mechanisms: Simple Password, Keyed MD5, Meticulous Keyed MD5, Keyed SHA-1 and Meticulous Keyed SHA-1. The simple password travels in plain text, so an eavesdropper can learn it. The keyed ones use a shared secret, and every packet carries a non-decreasing 32-bit sequence number. In the plain keyed modes the number only needs to increase occasionally; in the meticulous modes it must increase with each packet.

Key updating is limited: there is a Key ID in each packet but no described way to roll smoothly from one key to another. A 32-bit space can also run out. If the number rises by one every 3.3 milliseconds, it reaches its maximum in less than 24 weeks.

Each node picks a 32-bit discriminator, and a session is identified by two of them. In some deployments they come from the addresses, so after a rollover (for example a reboot) a new session can reuse the same pair. BFD echo packets have no defined format, and the specification gives no guidance on how to secure them.
sections.eli5: Each message gets a number that only goes up, like numbered tickets. The tickets are limited, and if the counter restarts, old tickets may look new.

sections.title: The Impact of Replay Attacks
sections.content:
In Keyed MD5 and Keyed SHA-1, the sequence number need not change each packet, so an attacker can replay the latest packet until it does. Meticulous modes remove this issue. After a rollover without automatic key management, an attacker can replay a packet with a larger number; if accepted, the victim rejects legitimate packets with smaller numbers, so the session can come down. The attack assumes access to the link, or the ability to inject packets for a multihop session.

BFD can also change state based on a received packet. If an accepted packet says the state is down, the receiver goes down too, so a carefully chosen replayed packet can cause a serious DoS. With identical discriminators and the same key in two successive sessions, a stored authenticated packet from the past can be replayed. For echo mode, guessable packets might be spoofed to make a one-way link look bidirectional, so echo packets should contain random material that is checked on reception.
sections.eli5: A copycat records a real message and plays it back later to trick the receiver, such as a fake goodbye that makes it hang up.

sections.title: The Cost of Stronger Authentication
sections.content:
Hardware BFD runs with timeouts of a few milliseconds; the RFC's example is a 3.3 millisecond timeout, meaning 3 packets every 10 milliseconds. Software typically runs with timeouts in the hundreds of milliseconds. Hardware support for computing the authentication data is not common.

In the non-meticulous modes, software can compute the hash if the interval between sequence-number increases is long enough. With the meticulous modes and short intervals it is difficult, and worse with hundreds or thousands of sessions. As a general rule, no more than 40 to 45 percent of the CPU can go to BFD, which can be exceeded with a few tens of authenticated sessions on smaller boxes. Implementors should assess the impact on their platform.
sections.eli5: Checking a secret stamp on every single message is slow. If a small computer has to check thousands of stamps a second, it runs out of energy for everything else.

sections.title: Suggested Improvements and Security Notes
sections.content:
The RFC suggests GMAC, the Galois Message Authentication Code, as a candidate that balances algorithm strength against overhead; it is supported by IPsec for data origin authentication (RFC 4543). It also mentions "hallway conversation" about authenticating only packets where BFD payload data changes, since most packets carry no state change. It says this needs more discussion in the BFD working group.

For replay, its security section notes that making the sequence number 64 bits long makes the wrap-around time much longer, so replay attacks can be easily prevented. The document discusses weaknesses and possible mitigations; it does not itself change BFD.
sections.eli5: Two ideas: use a faster strong lock, and only check the important messages instead of every one. Neither is final yet.
